tagline: A river road reaches Lolo Pass after decades of construction.
intro: US 12 follows the Clearwater River from Lewiston, crossing between its banks before climbing beside the Lochsa into the Bitterroot Mountains. The Northwest Passage Scenic Byway is an All-American Road; the Federal Highway Administration’s archived description emphasizes rivers, deep canyons and rugged mountains in Nez Perce country. That description gives six hours for driving the entire 202-mile byway.

The Lolo Trail crossing was already in use by Nez Perce in the eighteenth century, and carried Lewis and Clark west in 1805. The modern highway took decades to complete. Designated State Highway 9 in 1916, the Lewis and Clark Highway entered construction in 1920. Federal prisoners worked on it in the late 1930s and early 1940s; Japanese internees from Kooskia Internment Camp worked on it during the last two years of World War II. Completion came in 1962, when the road became US 12.

Driving east from Lewiston, follow the Clearwater through Orofino and Kamiah, then toward the junction with Idaho 13 across the river from Kooskia. Idaho 13 reaches Grangeville on the Camas Prairie. At Lowell, the Selway and Lochsa join to form the Middle Fork Clearwater. US 12 turns northeast along the Lochsa and crosses into Montana at Lolo Pass, 5,233 feet above sea level.

moments.title: Orofino
moments.text: Near Orofino, the Lewis and Clark expedition exchanged an overland journey for travel by dugout canoe. At Canoe Camp, five miles downstream from town, the party built five canoes and departed toward the Pacific on October 7, 1805. From Canoe Camp, their downstream journey reached the Columbia Bar and the Pacific Ocean about six weeks later. Orofino’s later transport connection ran on rails: the railroad from Lewiston was built in 1899 and later became part of the Camas Prairie Railroad. The town lies along Orofino Creek and the Clearwater’s north bank.

moments.title: Heart of the Monster
moments.text: For the nimíipuu, or Nez Perce, this landmark near Kamiah is a creation site. The National Park Service tells of Iceye’ye, coyote, killing a monster that was eating the animals. An interpretive shelter presents part of the story through exhibits and audio in Nez Perce and English. A short trail leads to the feature and a semicircle of seats. At the semicircle, another audio recording tells the Coyote and the Monster story in English beside the landmark itself. The park asks visitors to honor this spiritual place and leave its rock features undisturbed.

moments.title: Lolo Pass
moments.text: A cedar log served as the ceremonial barrier when the highway was dedicated at Lolo Pass in August 1962. Idaho governor Bob Smylie and Montana governor Tim Babcock cut it with a two-man crosscut saw. The older Lolo Trail also crosses this pass. Nez Perce used the trail in the eighteenth century; Old Toby of the Shoshone guided Lewis and Clark along it westward in September 1805. The expedition returned the following June. At 5,233 feet, the pass lies on the Idaho–Montana boundary in the Bitterroot Range of the northern Rocky Mountains.
